title: Pulling Apart Operational Data
subtitle: Separate data only when the system can carry the cost
summary: Pip separates delivery services, but reporting still consumes their shared database connections. Data ownership, transactions, and relationships make the next cut harder. The crew measures pressure, defines domains, and exposes hidden cross-schema dependencies before choosing new storage.

concepts.title: Disintegration drivers
concepts.body: Pip watches reporting consume connections until parcel intake times out. A shared database can block independent change, scale, availability, quantum separation, or workload-specific technology. Those are disintegration drivers, not proof that splitting is correct. Pip weighs measured contention against data relationships and transactions that may need to stay together.

concepts.title: Bounded data contracts
concepts.body: Pip renames a storage column and a neighboring service breaks. The owner should control writes and expose a contract, not its schema. Pip preserves the response field while changing internal representation within the bounded context. Direct cross-schema access would keep the accidental shared contract alive.

concepts.title: Connection and scale
concepts.body: Pip budgets 100 database connections for five services. Scaling to fourteen instances in the chapter’s example consumes 242: every instance brings its pool. Pip starts with quotas, measures waits and maximum use, then reallocates by need. Quotas must account for instance counts and cannot replace a database scaling plan.

concepts.title: Five step extraction
concepts.body: Pip defines data domains, assigns tables, and removes cross-domain artifacts. Service access moves to domain schemas before those schemas become physical databases. Local keys and views can remain; cross-domain joins, triggers, procedures, and views need explicit integration. Pip replaces a hidden customer join with an owner’s API.

concepts.title: Choose data technology
concepts.body: Pip keeps payment relationships in relational storage and evaluates documents for articles. Key-value favors lookup, graphs traversal, column families wide distributed access, and time-series timestamped measurements. NewSQL and cloud-native choices balance relational behavior against operational goals. Pip chooses within an understood domain seam; comparative adoption guidance is not a universal technology ranking.

concepts.title: Aggregate boundaries
concepts.body: Pip edits a survey and its questions together. One aggregate can preserve that atomic change when their lifecycle is shared. Reusable or independently administered questions may instead need references and explicit consistency rules. Pip follows how data loads and changes, avoiding a giant record merely because tables are related.

misconceptions.claim: A microservices migration always requires an immediate database-per-service split.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter allows staged data domains and shared database arrangements where appropriate. Decomposition should follow evidence from coupling, scale, availability, and transaction needs.

misconceptions.claim: Removing every foreign key is the first step to independent services.
misconceptions.correction: Local integrity artifacts can remain inside a data domain. Only cross-domain relationships need to be removed or replaced, and the migration is iterative.

scenario.title: Choose a data boundary
scenario.context: A support platform is moving from one relational database to domain services. Reporting causes connection waits, payment updates require atomic writes, and the knowledge base has document-shaped content. The database team has limited migration capacity and will accept only a reversible first slice. Decide what to separate first while preserving operational safety.

options.label: Reporting first
options.benefit: Directly addresses measured connection contention and reduces load on ticketing.
options.cost: The team must replace cross-domain reporting joins and operate another data store.
options.consequence: Reporting moves behind a domain schema and read contract. Ticketing remains on the original store while connection waits are measured again, giving the next extraction a clearer baseline.

options.label: Payment first
options.benefit: Keeps the strongest transaction boundary explicit and protects sensitive payment data.
options.cost: It may not relieve the immediate reporting bottleneck, and payment’s relationships require careful artifact refactoring.
options.consequence: Payment tables and local constraints move together. The migration improves ownership but users still see report timeouts until a later slice addresses reporting load.

scenario.debrief: The drivers point in different directions. A good first slice combines measurable benefit, a coherent domain, and a migration path that preserves required transactions. Technology choice follows the boundary; it should not substitute for one.

quiz.question: Which observation is strongest evidence for a connection-management disintegrator?
options: A table has a descriptive name
Service instances experience connection waits and request timeouts
Two tables have a foreign key
quiz.explanation: Connection waits and timeout symptoms indicate that distributed pools are exhausting the shared database capacity. A foreign key is instead an integration concern.

quiz.question: What should happen to a foreign key crossing two extracted data domains?
options: Preserve it invisibly across both databases
Remove it and make the relationship explicit through an integration mechanism
Duplicate it in every service schema
quiz.explanation: Cross-domain database artifacts preserve hidden coupling. The chapter’s process removes them and moves access behind service or other explicit boundaries.

quiz.question: Why evaluate instance counts when assigning connection quotas?
options: Quotas apply once to the whole cluster
Each instance can create a pool, so scale-out multiplies total connections
quiz.explanation: A quota that fits one instance per service can exceed database capacity after independent scale-out.

exercise.prompt: Draw one data domain from an existing schema, list its local artifacts, mark each cross-domain dependency, and justify the first migration step using one disintegrator and one integrator.
